Words you might not know

Some of the words used here come out of research and are not everyday English, and every one of them is explained in plain language at the back. Words that appear like this are in the glossary, and tapping one will take you straight there, with a link to bring you back to where you were.
Go to the glossary
Where to next
The next section explains how each of the eleven need sections is put together and how the different prompts are meant to work. Read it once before you start on Life.
Go to How to Use This Workbook

Every one of the eleven need sections is laid out the same way, and once you have been through the first one you will know your way around the rest. The kind of question you are asked changes between sections. Asking the same question eleven times produces eleven identical answers that nobody believes.
How each need section works

Every section opens with an explanation of what that need means, followed by two lists showing what it looks like when it is going well and when it is not. A panel then explains why that need matters for someone in your position. After that come eight boxes for you to fill in, and each box has a heading, an explanation of what it is asking for, a prompt to help you get started, and a space to write.

Work through the eight boxes in order. Several of them build on the ones before, and a sensible warning sign in box 6 is very hard to write if you have not yet worked out in box 2 why the need matters to you.
The eight boxes
1. Rate your ability

A number from 0 to 10 showing how well the need is being met in your life at the moment. A high number is not the aim. The number shows at a glance which areas need attention first, and gives you something to compare against at your next review.
2. Why this matters to me

What the need means in your own life. A plan built on things you think you are supposed to care about tends to give way the first time it is tested, with nothing behind it. Work out what is behind yours.
3. This need and my offending

Some needs will have been tangled up in your offending and some will not, and either answer is fine. Write about the state you were in, what you were feeling and what you were chasing, and leave out the behaviour itself. Answering truthfully here shows you where the repair work needs to go.
4. Steps to meet this need
The practical part, and the one that changes your week. These are things you are going to do, written down in enough detail that somebody else could tell whether you had done them or not.
5. Signs of success
How you will know it is working. Progress in these areas is slow and easy to miss, and if you cannot see yourself getting anywhere you may stop trying, so do not skip this box.
6. Signs of concern
Your early warnings. The aim is to spot a slide in the first week. By the eighth week it has usually taken a few other things down with it.
7. Response to concern
What you will do when a warning sign shows up, decided now while things are steady. On the day you need it, you will not be in a state to think one up from scratch.
8. Progress, changes and support
Left mostly empty at first and filled in at each review. It turns the workbook from a document you wrote once into a record of what has happened since.
The different kinds of prompt
The prompts change from section to section, partly to stop it turning into a form-filling exercise and partly because different questions suit different needs. Here is what each kind is for.
Questions to think about
A list of questions coming at one thing from different angles. Pick the two or three that start you thinking, answer those in full, and leave the rest alone.
Sentence starters

A line with gaps in it, such as “When I feel __________, what I usually do is __________”. The gaps stay empty on the page, and you read the sentence, work out how you would finish it, then write the full sentence in the box underneath. The gaps give you a frame for your answer when you are not sure how to start.
Check your answer

A short checklist that you apply to your own answer after you have written it. Write first, then read your answer back against the list and fix whatever fails. It works like a tradesman checking his own work before somebody else sees it.
Word banks

A run of single words separated by slashes, covering the ground that a need takes in. Use them to jog your memory about areas you might not have considered. Never write the words down as your answer. On their own they are too vague for anybody to act on.
Notes
Asides that flag a common mistake in that box. Read them. They will usually save you redoing your writing later.
Worked examples

A few sections include an example written by somebody else, set deliberately on its own separate page, apart from the box. Read it once to see the level you are aiming for, then go back and write your own from scratch. If your answer ends up looking like the example, you have written somebody else’s plan, and it will not hold up when you need it to.
Using it well
A few habits make this more useful.
Write it in your own words, including the awkward ones. Language borrowed from group, from a court report or from a book you half remember will sound fine and mean nothing to you in six months.
Give names, days, times and places for everything. “Regularly” and “more often” are intentions with the useful part left out.
Do not save the hard sections for later. Later often does not arrive. If a section is uncomfortable, that is usually a sign it is one you most need to do.
If you have a group or someone you trust, take it to them. The sections get better once somebody else has asked you a question about them.
Do not aim for a workbook that looks impressive. Aim for one that would still make sense to you on your worst week of the year, the week you will be reading it.
Help with reading and writing

This part can be difficult, whatever you have to say. If you have a psychologist, tell them early, before you end up with a workbook full of one-line answers that do not help you. Short answers are fine, and you can return to a box later.
Someone you trust can read the sections out to you and write what you say.
You can answer out loud and type up short notes afterwards, or record yourself and work from that.
You can pair up with someone you trust, with one of you asking the questions and the other answering, and then swap over.
Short answers are fine. Six true words beat six polished lines that you copied from somewhere.
Where to start

Start at the beginning with Life, and go through the eleven needs in order. They are arranged so that the more concrete ones come before the ones that take more thinking, and by the time you reach the harder sections you will have had some practice.
Go to Step 1, getting started Go straight to the first need, Life

Life means being well in your body and your mind. It covers the upkeep of being a person: sleeping, eating, moving your body, whatever you drink or take, going to the doctor when something is wrong, and feeling reasonably alright in your own skin.

Life sits first because the other needs depend on it, and when it gives way the rest tend to go with it. Poor sleep alone will flatten your mood, shorten your temper and make it hard to concentrate. It makes every other need in this workbook harder to meet, and you cannot think your way out of being exhausted.

This need covers the physical side of things and also how you feel about your body and your health, and the two do not always match. Two men with identical blood pressure can feel completely differently about themselves. Write about both here.
Signs of progress
You sleep most nights, and you wake up feeling rested.
You eat at roughly normal times on most days, without having to think about it much.
Your body moves regularly in some way, whether that is a gym or a walk.
Alcohol and anything else you use do not decide how your evenings go.
You go to the doctor when something is wrong, within a few weeks.
You do not particularly dread what you see in the mirror.
Signs of drifting
You are up half the night and flat all the following day, and each of those two things keeps feeding the other.
You eat whatever happens to be nearest, or you barely eat at all, or you eat mainly because you are bored.
Weeks go past without you leaving the house for any reason that was not compulsory.
You drink to get yourself off to sleep, or to stop yourself thinking about something.
You have a pain or symptom that you have decided to ignore, sometimes for years.
Why this need matters

Poor sleep, low mood and a body that has stopped being looked after do not cause anybody to offend, and plenty of exhausted, unwell people never harm anyone at all. What those things do is wear down the part of you that stops and thinks before acting. The decisions you make at two in the morning, tired and flat and on your own, are not the ones you would make at ten on a Saturday after a walk and a decent night’s sleep. Look back for a stretch where your health fell apart before things went wrong. Knowing that about yourself excuses nothing, and it gives you a pattern you can learn to watch for.

Eight boxes follow, each a different way into the question. Some ask you to finish a sentence, some ask you to test what you have already written, and some ask a question from an unusual angle. Work through them in order.
1. Rate your ability
Before you pick a number, decide what your own 10 would look like. A 6 has no meaning until you do.
Set your own scale first
Write these three in your own words, and keep them realistic. A 10 is not perfect health or the body you had at twenty-two, but the best this could be for you, at your age, with the life you have.
Describe what a 0 for Life looks like for you, in your own words.
Describe what a 5 for Life looks like for you.
Describe what a 10 for Life looks like for you. Not perfect health, just the best this could be at your age.
Rate where you are today
Rate Life as it stands today, 0 to 10, where 0 means the need is not met at all and 10 means it is fully met.
A low number here is information. Low scores tell you where the work needs to start. A page full of 8s and 9s often means the person has not looked hard yet.
2. Why this matters to me
Say why health matters to you this year. Knowing that sleep is good for the body has never changed anyone’s behaviour on its own.
Questions to think about
Pick whichever two or three of these questions get something moving in your head, answer those ones properly, and ignore the rest without feeling bad about it.
Describe an ordinary Tuesday when your body and your head both felt right. What was in that day?
What could you do at twenty-five that you cannot do now, and does losing that bother you, or have you made your peace with it?
Who else is affected when your health starts to slide, and which of them notices it before you do?
If a doctor gave you one piece of news next week that made you change something immediately, what would that news have to be?
What would “enough” look like in this area? Not the ideal version of it, just enough to be going on with.
3. This need and my offending

For some men the answer to this is no, and no is a complete answer. For others there is a clear link, and this is the place to write it. Either way, write what was going on in your body and your head in the lead up to it, not the behaviour itself.
Write about how you felt, what you wanted and what you were thinking at the time. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
In the months before things went wrong, my sleep was __________ and my drinking was __________.
Physically I felt __________ on most days, and looking back at it now, the first thing that started to slide was __________.
When I was feeling like that, what I wanted was __________.
The behaviour gave me __________, which I was not getting anywhere else in my life at that point.
If my health had been in better shape back then, what might have been different is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Life need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Writing down a link here excuses nothing, and being tired or unwell causes no one to offend. It shows you where the repair work needs to start, and a plan that ignores the state you were in has no foundation. See how one man answered this box
4. Steps to meet this need
What you write here changes what your week looks like. Everything before it was thinking, and this part is doing.
Pick your area
Pick two or three of the areas below that you want to work on, and do not write those words as your answer. On their own they are too vague to act on.
sleep / alcohol / walking / food / water / screens at night / GP / dentist / medication / teeth / weight / smoking / back / knees / hearing / eyes / daylight / routine / caffeine / mornings
Make each a weekly action
Every step you write needs to have four things in it. Write your steps out first, then read them back against this list and fix any that fail.
a.	A what, the action itself, such as “walk” and not the outcome “get fitter”.
b.	A when, a day or a time you could put in your phone, such as “each morning before work” or “Tuesday and Thursday”.
c.	A where or who, a place or a person’s name.
d.	A step you will do, and if you have written something to stop, add what will fill the space it leaves behind.
Aim for two or three steps. Three steps you carry out will do more for you than ten you read once and never look at again.
Write two or three steps for Life. Each one needs a what, a when, and a where or a who, and each has to be something you will do, not something you will stop.
5. Signs of success
Decide now how you will know that any of this is working. Progress you cannot see is easy to stop working on.
Ask it from outside yourself
You are with yourself every day and your gradual improvement is too slow to see up close, but other people spot it much better, so answer these as though you were them.
Think of someone who sees you every week. What would they notice first, and would they say something about it or just think it?
Think of someone who knows you well, such as your psychologist, three months from now. What would have to be different for them to say that this one has shifted?
Think of yourself in six months looking back at today. What is the unglamorous thing you would tell yourself to keep doing?

Be wary of signs that only exist inside your own head, such as “feeling more positive about things”, which nobody else can see and neither can you on a bad day. Look for things that could be noticed from the outside.
6. Signs of concern
These are your early warnings. Write them down so you catch a slide in week one, when it is much easier to pull back from than in week eight.
Trace back a bad stretch
Think of a stretch when your health fell away badly, whether or not it had anything to do with your offending, and run that period backwards.
Once it was clearly bad and you could not pretend otherwise, what was happening in your days?
Two weeks before that point, what had already changed? A late night or a skipped meal counts.
What was the first thing to go? It may be one dropped routine.
Did anyone say anything to you at the time, and if they did, what did you tell them?
That first thing to go is your warning sign. Write it in a form you could check. “Three nights in a row where I did not get to sleep before two” can be checked, and “feeling a bit off” cannot.
7. Response to concern
Write this one now, while things are steady. It belongs in the plan because you will not be in a state to invent a response on the day you need one.
Build it as if-then
An if-then plan makes the decision in advance, leaving nothing to talk yourself out of when the moment arrives.
If I notice __________, then within __________ I will __________.
The person I will tell is __________, and I will tell them by __________ (a text, a phone call, or in person).
If I cannot get hold of them, my second person is __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not doing any of this is __________, and my answer to that excuse is __________.
Spend the longest on that last stem. You probably have a standard excuse that you use without noticing, and writing it down now takes most of its power away.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Life? Write one response for the first sign and a faster one if it keeps going.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, and return to it at every review. That turns the workbook from a document you wrote once into a record of what happened.
Build on what worked
You are not starting from zero here, even if it feels that way at the moment.
Give one occasion in the last month when this need was met even slightly, whether that was one decent night’s sleep or one walk.
What made that possible? Think about where you were, what time it was, who else was involved and what was different about that particular day.
What would it take to make that happen twice as often? The answer may be smaller and more boring than you expect.
Review questions
What has improved since the last review? Give an example you could point to, and be fair to yourself.
Which step did not happen? Was it the wrong step, or just the wrong week?
What support do you need that you are not currently getting, who could provide it, and have you asked them yet?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps has a what, a when, and either a where or a who.
At least one of those steps could start this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about being free of stress and emotional turmoil, and being able to sit still in your own company without something churning away underneath. It covers stress, worry, anger, guilt and shame, and it also covers whether you have any reliable way of settling yourself down when those things turn up.

Everyone has difficult feelings, and this need does not ask you to be calm all the time. It asks whether difficult feelings pass through when they arrive, and whether you have a way to deal with them that is neither swallowing them nor acting on them.

It also covers feeling safe, both physically and in the sense of not spending your days braced for the next thing to go wrong. You may look calm from the outside and still live with a background tension you have got used to, to the point where you no longer notice it and would not know what its absence felt like.
Signs of progress
You can sit on your own for an hour without needing something to distract you from your own head.
When something goes wrong, you feel it and it passes within days.
You have two or three things you can reliably do that bring you back down, and you do them.
You can tell somebody that you are struggling before it reaches the point of a crisis.
You are not lying awake running arguments you have already had.
Signs of drifting
You are tense most of the time without being able to point at a particular reason for it.
Small things set you off, and afterwards you cannot explain the size of the reaction, even to yourself.
Silence is uncomfortable, and you need something on in the background at all times.
Feelings get pushed down and stored until something eventually knocks the lid off.
Your only reliable way of switching off is one you would rather other people did not know about.
That last line is the reason this need sits so early in the workbook. Stop on it before you go on.
Why this need matters

Think back to any stress or emptiness you had no idea how to shift, and whether a behaviour switched it off completely for a couple of hours. If it did, it was chosen less because it was appealing than because it worked, quickly and reliably, in a life where nothing else did. If you take away the one thing that worked without replacing it, the problem is still there. You have made the pressure worse and removed the valve.
Eight boxes again, with different prompts from the ones in Life.
1. Rate your ability
This one moves around more than most, so a single number for today tells you little. Rate it at three points and pay attention to the difference between them.
Rate three points in time
Rate Inner peace as it was about a year ago, 0 to 10.
Rate Inner peace as it was about a month ago, 0 to 10.
Rate Inner peace as it stands today, 0 to 10.
Now explain the gaps
If those three numbers are different from each other, something changed them, and knowing what changed them tells you more than the numbers do.
If those three numbers are different from each other, what changed between them?
If all three numbers came out the same, check whether that is true or whether you picked a number and stuck with it. A year is a long time for nothing to change.
2. Why this matters to me
Do not stop at describing what stress feels like, which everybody already knows. Write about what it costs you and what it gets in the way of.
Sentence starters
When I am wound up, the first person to cop it is __________, and what they get from me is __________.
The thing I stop doing when I am stressed is __________.
If I had one settled month, the thing I would finally get around to is __________.
I have been carrying __________ for about __________ years now.
What I want here is not to feel nothing but __________.
Why does Inner peace matter to you? Write what you want here, even if it is different from what you think you should want.
3. This need and my offending
You may answer yes to this, and see that your offending hinged on it. Take your time.
Write about what you were feeling, what you wanted and what you were trying to get away from. Do not describe the offending.
Questions to think about
Pick the two or three of these that get something moving, and answer those properly.
What was the feeling you were trying to get away from? Give it a name, even a clumsy one, and be more precise than “stressed” if you can.
How long did the relief last afterwards, and what did the hour after that feel like?
What else had you tried before this, and why did those things not work or not last?
Was it about feeling something, or about feeling nothing for a while? Those are two different things and they lead to different plans.
If somebody had asked you at the time whether you were stressed, what would you have told them?

Understanding that a behaviour worked as a way of coping is not excusing it, and it does not make it any less harmful to the people affected by it. It tells you what your plan has to replace, and a plan with nothing in its place will not last. See how one man answered this box
4. Steps to meet this need
Writing down five or six calming things you have heard of and never done is the trap here. Write only the few you will use on a bad day.
List more than you need
Write six things that might settle you down. Include the obvious ones and the daft ones, and do not filter anything out yet.
Rank them

Now review your six and put them in order using this question: which of these would I do at nine o’clock at night, on my own, feeling terrible, with no one watching?
Keep the top two or three and cross the rest out. A short list you use beats a long list you admire.
Check what is left
a.	It can be started in under five minutes.
b.	It does not depend on anybody else being available at the time.
c.	It works in the place you will be on a bad day.
d.	You have done it at least once already and know that it does something for you.
You also need one step that prevents the pressure building up. Something regular and unremarkable, like a standing Wednesday walk, does more over a year than any emergency technique.
Write two or three steps for Inner peace, including one that stops the pressure building up.
5. Signs of success
Progress here is slow and mostly invisible, which makes it very easy to conclude that nothing is happening when quite a lot is.
Write from six months ahead
Imagine it is six months from now and this has gone reasonably well, though not perfectly. Describe an ordinary week from inside it.
What do your evenings look like in that week, hour by hour, from getting home to going to bed?
Something goes wrong on the Wednesday. What do you do with it, and how long does it take you to get past it?
What has stopped happening that used to happen every week without fail?
What would somebody who has not seen you for six months say when they saw you?
Write what you would notice. “I got to sleep before midnight most nights” can be checked against a real week, and “I felt calmer in myself” cannot.
6. Signs of concern
Stress shows up in three separate places, and you may only watch one of them. The one you notice last is usually the one that would have warned you earliest.
Check all three places
Write at least one warning sign under each of these three headings. If you cannot think of anything under one of them, ask somebody who knows you well, who will have noticed signs you have not.
In your body
Jaw, shoulders, stomach, sleep, appetite, headaches, that feeling in the chest. Look for where it shows up in you first.
In your thinking
Running the same argument over and over, everything feeling pointless, black and white thinking, or telling yourself that nobody would care anyway.
In what you do
Not answering the phone, cancelling things, drinking earlier in the day, being short with people, staying up later and later, or going quiet around other people.
What would be the first sign that Inner peace is slipping? Write something somebody could check.
7. Response to concern
You probably know what you ought to do when the pressure comes on, and at that moment it may all seem pointless. Write your answer as advice to someone else.
Write to somebody else first
Picture a man, six months in, who has gone quiet. He is not sleeping, he has stopped going to things and he says there is no point ringing anybody because they have their own problems.
What would you say to him? Write it properly, in your own words.
What would you tell him to do first, tonight, before he does anything else?
He says he does not want to be a burden. What is your answer to that?
Now read back what you have written. How much of it applies to you, and what stops you taking your own advice?
Then make it a plan
If I notice __________, then within __________ I will __________.
The person I will tell is __________, and if I cannot reach them my second person is __________.
8. Progress, changes and support
Build on what you handled
You may have a poor record of what you have already handled. The bad stretches are memorable and the ordinary coping is not.
Pick a difficult day in the last month that you got through without anything going wrong. What did you do that day?
Who or what helped, even a little, and did you tell them afterwards that it had?
What does that tell you about which of your steps is working?
Review questions
Has your rating changed, and if so, what changed it? If it went down, write that down.
Which of your calming steps did you use, and which one turned out to be theoretical?
What support do you need that you are not getting, and have you asked for it yet?
Final check
Your steps include at least one thing that prevents pressure building, not only things that deal with it afterwards.
Every step could be started in five minutes on a bad night.
You have a warning sign in your body, one in your thinking, and one in what you do.
Your response gives one person and a backup person.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about hobbies, interests, fun, and being good at something. It covers what you do with the hours that are yours, and whether any of them give you something to look forward to. It takes in sport, music, fishing, cars, gardening, games, building things and anything else that you do because you want to.

Fun is a good enough reason on its own, and this need covers it. It also covers getting better at a skill over time. That kind of satisfaction comes only from being less bad at it than you were last year. Watching television or scrolling does not give you that feeling.

The other half of this need is balance. If your life is all work and obligation with nothing in it for you, you will eventually look for something, and you may not look sensibly. Adults are bad at this, and somewhere along the way you may decide that having interests is for teenagers and stop replacing the ones you lose.
Signs of progress
You have at least one thing in your week that you would be annoyed about having to cancel.
You are getting better at something, even slowly, and you could describe how.
Some of what you do involves other people, and some of it is just yours.
Your free time gets used on purpose.
You could answer the question “what are you into” without having to think about it for a while.
Signs of drifting
Evenings and weekends run together into one long stretch with nothing in them you would remember afterwards.
The things you used to do have stopped, usually without any decision being made.
Boredom is a constant background hum.
Your free time goes mostly to a screen, and you would rather not add up how much.
Somebody asks what you do for yourself and you cannot come up with anything.
If the second list fits you better than the first, give this section more time than it seems to need.
Why this need matters

Empty time is not a risk factor in itself, but other risk factors build on it. Think back to how things built up and look for long stretches of unstructured evening time, alone, with nothing much to do and nothing to look forward to. Boredom is more uncomfortable than it sounds, and an uncomfortable person will reach for whatever is closest and easiest. Building a week that has things in it is one of the most practical parts of the plan.
Eight boxes, and the prompts differ again from the last two. Work through them in order.
1. Rate your ability
Rate it twice and compare them, which tells you more than either number does by itself.
Now, and back then
Rate Excellence in play as it is met today, 0 to 10.
Rate Excellence in play as it was met when you were about sixteen, 0 to 10.
What happened in between
If you score much lower now than you did then, ask what took the old hobbies away and whether any of those reasons still apply.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Not having the time can be a reason or an excuse. Before you write anything, read the two statements below.
Reasons and excuses
I would like to have more going on, but between work and everything else there is not much time for it at the moment.
Between getting home at half five and going to bed at eleven I have five and a half hours, and at the moment almost none of it is spent on anything I would miss.

Both of those could be written by the same person on the same evening. The first closes the subject down and the second opens it up with numbers that can be argued with. Write your answer in the second style.
How many hours of your own do you have in a normal week? Add them up roughly.
Where do those hours currently go? List each activity.
What did you used to be into, and what did you like about it? Not the activity, the feeling underneath it.
What would you want to be able to say you were good at in three years?
3. This need and my offending
You may not think boredom caused your offending, and you do not have to say it did. Write what the empty time was doing, which may have been the setting and not the cause.
Write about your time, your boredom and what you were looking for. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
In the year before things went wrong, the last thing I did purely because I enjoyed it was __________.
My evenings back then went like this: __________.
The hours where it happened were usually __________, and what I would otherwise have been doing at that time was __________.
It gave me something to do, and what it replaced was __________.
If I had had one thing in my week I looked forward to, what might have been different is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Excellence in play need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.
4. Steps to meet this need
Plans fail here when you write down an ambitious step that you never begin. Plan for the obstacle. It will turn up.
Jog your memory
Use these areas to remind yourself of things you have not thought about in years. Do not write any of these words down as your step.

fishing / cards / guitar / bikes / running / bowls / darts / dogs / veggie garden / restoring something / woodwork / photography / cooking / chess / model building / swimming / walking group / choir / motorbikes / metal detecting / footy / volunteering / drawing / reading
Plan for obstacles
For each step you write, add the thing most likely to stop it and what you will do about that. A step written without its obstacle is a wish.
I will __________ on __________ at __________. The thing most likely to stop this is __________, and if that happens I will __________.
Check your answer
a.	At least one step costs nothing.
b.	At least one step involves other people, since anything done entirely alone is very easy to drop.
c.	At least one step is an activity you could get better at over time.
d.	Every step has a day attached to it. Not a frequency, a day.

Pick things that are already running to a schedule somebody else sets, such as a club night or a class. Turning up to something that happens at seven on a Thursday whether you come or not is far easier than organising yourself from scratch every week.
Write two or three steps for Excellence in play, preferring things that already run to a schedule somebody else sets.
5. Signs of success
Success in this area shows up in your calendar before it shows up in how you feel, which makes it easier to check than most.
Describe the week
Describe what you would be doing in a good week six months from now.
Which nights of the week have something in them, and what?
What would somebody see if they looked in your shed, your kitchen or the boot of your car?
Who would you have spoken to that week who is not family and not from group?
What are you better at than you were six months ago, and how would you demonstrate it?
6. Signs of concern
Things rarely stop with a decision. They stop with a reason that sounds sensible at the time, so write it down in advance.
Write your excuses first
You probably have three or four standard lines you use when you are about to drop something. Write yours down now, while you are not using them.
What did you tell yourself last time you stopped going to something? Use the actual words.
How many weeks in a row would you have to miss before you had stopped going altogether?
What is the first thing to disappear from your week when you are not doing well?
Who would notice, and would they say anything?
Turn the answers into something checkable. “Two Thursdays missed in a row” is a warning sign you can act on. “Losing interest” tends to be recognised only long after it has happened.
7. Response to concern
When you restart something you have dropped, the full version feels like too much and you may do nothing. Decide now what the smallest possible version looks like.
Write the two-minute version
For each of your steps, work out the smallest version that still counts as doing it. Not the good version, the version you could not talk yourself out of.
Instead of __________, the smallest version is __________, which takes about __________ minutes.
If I have missed __________ in a row, then I will __________ before the next one comes around.
The person I will tell is __________, and what I will ask them to do is __________.

Walking to the end of the street counts as a walk. Ten minutes on the guitar counts as playing. The smallest version keeps the thing going, and a habit that is still going can be built back up, while one that has stopped has to be started again from the beginning.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Excellence in play? Write one response for the first sign and a faster one if it keeps going.
8. Progress, changes and support
Sort what you have tried

By your first review you will have tried some things, and some of them will not have taken. Something that did not take is not a failure. You learn from it when you sort what you tried by what happened.
Which things did you keep doing, and what did they have in common?
Which ones fell over, and why: the activity itself, the timing, the cost, or doing it alone?
Which one would you put your money on for the next six months, and what would make it more likely to stick?
Review questions
How many nights in a typical week now have something in them? Compare that with the last review.
Is there anything you are now noticeably better at?
What support would help, and who could provide it?
Final check
Every step has a day attached to it.
At least one step costs nothing and at least one involves other people.
You have written the obstacle for each step and what you will do about it.
You have a two-minute version of each step for the weeks when the full version is beyond you.
Your steps could not harm another person or put you at risk of offending, and anything that involves children fits your legal conditions and your safety plan. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: Spirituality here means meaning and purpose, whatever those mean to you, and it asks whether your life adds up to something and whether you could say what. Religion is part of it for some people, and the word is used here in a broader sense than usual.

Purpose in this sense is rarely grand. It has little to do with achievement or with leaving a mark on the world. Yours may be one of these: being a decent father, being the one who turns up when somebody needs a hand, keeping something going that would fall over without you, or looking after a bit of ground. What counts is whether it gives your weeks a meaning to you, however impressive it sounds.

Do not skip this need, even if the word puts you off or the question feels as though it has no answer. A person who cannot say what their life is for has no way to measure a decision, and is much easier to knock off course.
Signs of progress
You could say what matters to you and why, without having to make it up on the spot.
You have something in your life that you would keep doing even if nobody thanked you for it.
Your decisions mostly line up with what you say you believe, and where they do not, you notice.
Bad stretches sit inside something larger, which makes them hard without being pointless.
You have some sense of the kind of man you are trying to be, separate from what you have done.
Signs of drifting
One week is much like the next and none of them seem to be heading anywhere in particular.
You could not say what you believe about much of anything, and you have not thought about it in years.
Things that used to matter to you have stopped mattering, and there was no moment where you decided that.
You find yourself thinking that none of it makes any difference either way.
What you do and what you say you believe have come apart, and you avoid looking at the gap.
Why this need matters

Two things make this need pressing after offending. The first is drift. Someone who has no sense of what his life is for has no way to weigh a decision. Decisions get made on whatever feels all right at the time, and the choices add up in a direction nobody chose. The second is what happens afterwards. Offending tends to take away whatever sense of purpose a person had, and it can leave someone believing he is finished as a person and that nothing he does now counts. A man who thinks he has nothing left to protect has no reason to protect anything, and that is where the danger lies. Rebuilding a sense of purpose does not let you off, and it gives you something to stay on course for.
Eight boxes. Give this section more time than the last three and expect the first answers to come out messy.
1. Rate your ability
Two scales measure different things here. Look at the distance between them.
Rate how important having a sense of purpose is to you, 0 to 10.
Rate how well that need is met in your life at the moment, 0 to 10.
Look at the gap

A large gap between those two numbers means you know this need matters and are not meeting it. A low score on both needs the same attention. It usually means one of two things: either this need is not important to you, or it has been unmet for so long that you have stopped expecting anything from it.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Approaching this head on rarely works. Nobody can answer “what is your purpose in life” cold. Come at it sideways.
Questions to think about
Pick two or three of these, and take longer over them than you would in other sections.
Think of somebody you respect, alive or dead, whom you have met in person. What is it about how they live that you respect?
What would you want a grandchild to know about you? Not what you would want hidden, what you would want known.
What would you still do even if nobody ever found out you had done it?
When did you last feel useful to somebody? What were you doing?
If you had to write down three things you believe are true about how people ought to treat each other, what would they be?
What do you want to be able to say you spent your fifties, sixties or seventies doing?
If nothing comes, write that and raise it with your psychologist. “I have got nothing for this and it bothers me” is a complete answer and a better starting point than an invented one.
3. This need and my offending
The link here may be an absence of meaning. You may not say you offended in search of meaning, but you may recall a stretch beforehand where nothing seemed to matter much either way.
Write about what you believed, what you had stopped caring about and how you justified things to yourself. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
In that period, what I would have said my life was for is __________.
The things that used to matter to me that had stopped mattering were __________.
The way I squared it with myself at the time was __________.
What I believed about myself back then was __________.
What I believe about myself now is __________, and the difference between those two is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Spirituality need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the third stem, the hardest one on the page. Anyone who has done something he knew was wrong had some way of justifying it at the time. Being able to describe your own version is a large part of making sure it cannot be used again.
4. Steps to meet this need
Purpose is built from things you do repeatedly, and the steps you write here will look ordinary.
Areas for this need
Use these to jog your thinking, and write your own answer.

being useful to someone / looking after something living / faith or a religious community / cultural connection / country and land / mentoring / repairing something broken / giving time / caring for a relative / keeping a family thing going / study / craft / conservation / being reliable / telling the truth consistently
Small repeated actions
A step here should be something that happens more than once, that costs you something, and that you would still do if nobody noticed.
Because I believe __________, I will __________ every __________.
Check your answer
a.	It describes an action you take. Beliefs do not go in this box.
b.	It repeats. A one-off gesture does not build anything.
c.	It costs you time, effort or convenience.
d.	You would still do it if nobody ever knew about it.

One caution for this section. Wanting to be useful to others is good. Where children are already part of your life, check every step against your legal conditions and your safety plan, and do not write a step that seeks out new contact with children. If something on your list is heading that way, stop and talk to your psychologist before you write it down, and leave that step off the list.
Write two or three steps for Spirituality. Each one needs a what, a when, and a where or a who.
5. Signs of success
Look for consistency between what you say and what you do. That is how progress shows in this need.
Look for evidence
What in your week would somebody see as evidence of what you say matters to you?
When was the last time you did something inconvenient because it was the right thing to do? How often does that happen?
What have you kept going for more than three months without anybody making you?
If somebody asked you what you were about, could you answer without rehearsing it first?
6. Signs of concern
The warning signs here are mostly things you say to yourself, which makes them easy to miss. Write them down.
Thoughts you recognise
Read these and mark the ones you recognise. Then write the version you use, in your own words.
“None of this makes any difference anyway.”
“I am past it, there is no point starting anything now.”
“After what I have done, who am I to be talking about right and wrong.”
“Nobody would care either way.”

Look at the third one again. Feeling that you have forfeited the right to any values at all is dangerous. A man who believes he has nothing left to protect will not protect anything. Feeling ashamed of what you did and keeping to what you believe do not conflict, whatever it feels like.
7. Response to concern
Arguing yourself out of that kind of thinking on your own rarely works. The thinking is very good at answering back. Do something concrete, and tell somebody.
Say it to somebody else
Picture a man saying, out loud, that after what he has done there is no point in him trying to be any particular kind of person.
What would you say back to him? Write it in your own words.
What would you suggest he do this week, rather than think?
Now read it back. How much of that applies to you, and what stops you accepting it?
Then make it a plan
If I catch myself thinking __________, then I will __________ and I will tell __________.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, and expect your answer to change more between reviews than any other in the workbook.
Start from evidence
Give one thing you have done in the last month that you would want known about you.
What made that possible, and could you do it more often?
Has anything you believe changed in the last year? What changed it?
Review questions
Are you doing what you said you would? Where has the gap opened up between what you believe and what you do?
Has your answer to “what is my life for” changed, and is the new one closer to true?
Who could help with this, and would you be willing to have that conversation?
Final check
Your steps are things you do.
Each step repeats and each one costs you something.
Any step that involves children fits your legal conditions and your safety plan, and none of them seeks out new contact with children.
You have written down the words of the thinking that worries you, not a polite version of it.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about feeling good right now, in the moment, and enjoying something while it is happening. A decent feed, a hot shower after a cold day, sitting in the sun, laughing at something, the first ten minutes of a Saturday morning with nowhere to be.

It sounds like the least serious need on the list, and it is one of the most important. A life with no pleasure in it at all is not sustainable, and a person living one will eventually take pleasure from somewhere, sensibly or otherwise. Removing everything enjoyable from your life as a form of punishment is not a plan, it is a countdown.

Pleasures come in two kinds. Some are quick, intense and over in a moment, and they tend to leave you flatter than you were. Others are slower, milder and leave you better off afterwards. Both count, and a life built entirely from the first kind will keep needing a bigger dose.
Signs of progress
Most days have things that you enjoy while they are happening.
You notice them while they happen.
Enjoying something does not come with a layer of guilt on top of it.
You can stay in an everyday moment without needing it to be more than it is.
Most of what you enjoy is the slow kind.
Signs of drifting
Days go by in a flat grey with nothing in them either good or bad.
The only things that reliably do anything for you are quick, intense and over fast.
You feel you have no right to enjoy anything and do not let yourself.
You are mostly somewhere else in your head, either back in something that happened or ahead in something that might.
What used to be enough is no longer enough.
Why this need matters

This need connects to offending more directly than most, and in two opposite ways. The first is that online offending is, among other things, a quick and reliable way of producing a strong feeling, and a flat life goes looking for that. The second comes afterwards. You may have left court determined that you no longer deserve to enjoy anything, and stripped your life back to work, sleep and obligation. That feels like taking it seriously, and for a few months it lasts. Then the emptiness becomes unbearable. The plan, having ruled out enjoyment at the start, has no answer for it. Building pleasure back into your life does not let you off the hook, and it stops the pressure building to the point where something has to give.
Eight boxes. Saying that you miss enjoying things can be uncomfortable.
1. Rate your ability
Rate yourself, then have a go at rating yourself as somebody else would. The two ratings may be further apart than you expect.
Rate Happiness as you see it today, 0 to 10.
Rate Happiness as somebody who knows you well would rate it, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ
A higher self-rating often means you are counting things you no longer do. A lower one often means you are being harder on yourself than the evidence supports. Write a sentence about the gap.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Writing down that you want to enjoy your life can feel like asking for something you have forfeited. Write it anyway.
Questions to think about
What is the last thing you remember enjoying while it was happening? How long ago was that?
What did you cut out of your life after everything happened, and was cutting it out necessary, or did it just feel appropriate?
What do you tell yourself when you catch yourself enjoying something?
If a mate said he had decided he was never going to enjoy anything again, what would you think of that plan?
What is something harmless that you would like to have back?
3. This need and my offending
Write about the feeling you were chasing, how long it lasted and what came after it. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
What I was chasing was __________, and the closest everyday thing to that feeling is __________.
It lasted about __________, and afterwards I felt __________.
Over time I needed __________ to get the effect I used to get, which tells me __________.
Apart from this, the things in my life that gave me a lift were __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Happiness need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the third stem. Anything that needs to get bigger to keep working is a bad long-term arrangement, whatever it is, and seeing that pattern in yourself does more than resolve does. See how one man answered this box
4. Steps to meet this need
Build a life with enough everyday enjoyment in it that the flatness never gets bad enough to need rescuing.
List ten small things

Ten things you enjoy, or used to enjoy, that are harmless and cost little or nothing. If you are stuck, try these areas: food, weather, water, music, animals, being outside, warmth, a task finished, quiet, company.
Sort them by speed
Review your ten and mark each one.
Fast
Strong, quick, over in minutes, and you often want another one straight after. Sugar, a drink, a big spend, anything on a screen designed to keep you there.
Slow
Milder, takes longer to arrive, lasts afterwards, and does not leave you wanting more. A long walk, cooking properly, being in water, a proper conversation, working on something with your hands.
You do not have to get rid of the fast ones, and a life with none of them in it would be joyless. Aim for balance. If nine of your ten are fast, your plan needs the most work here.
Put three in your week
I will __________ on __________, which takes about __________ minutes.
a.	At least two of the three are the slow kind.
b.	Each one would survive a bad week.
c.	None of it needs anybody else’s permission or availability.
d.	You would be comfortable with anybody knowing about all of it.
Write two or three steps for Happiness, and check each one against the test that you would be comfortable with anybody knowing about all of it.
5. Signs of success
The change here is subtle, and it is much easier to spot in what you are not doing than in what you are.
What would somebody else notice
Somebody who sees you weekly. What would look different about you, and would they be able to say why?
What would they hear you talk about that you do not talk about now?
What would have stopped, that they might notice before you do?
Six months from now, what would you have looked forward to that week?
Enjoying something without immediately following it with a reason why you should not have is one of the better signs in this area, and a boring one.
6. Signs of concern
Watch for two different warnings here. They look like opposites, and it is easy to watch for one and miss the other.
Trace back a flat stretch
Think of a period when everything went grey on you. Run it backwards and find the first sign.
Once it was clearly bad, what did your days look like?
Two weeks earlier, what had already gone?
What was the first thing you stopped bothering with?
Then check the other direction
The second warning is the opposite of flatness, and it is the more serious of the two.
Is anything in your life needing to get bigger, longer or more frequent to do what it used to do?
Is there anything you enjoy that you have started keeping to yourself?
If either of those last two questions produced an answer, do not sit on it. Raise it with your psychologist this week, or write the date you noticed it and review it at your next review.
7. Response to concern
Write a different response for each of the two warnings.
Build both as if-then
If everything has gone flat and I notice __________, then I will __________ within __________ and tell __________.
If I notice something needing to get bigger to work, or notice myself keeping something to myself, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not following through is __________, and my answer to it is __________.

The second response has to be faster and less negotiable than the first, and it needs to go to somebody who can do something about it. The secrecy is the danger there, more than whatever is being kept secret.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Happiness? Write one response for the first sign and a faster, less negotiable one if it keeps going.
8. Progress, changes and support
Build on what worked
Write down one moment in the last week that you enjoyed while it was happening. It can be tiny.
What made it possible, and how hard would it be to have that twice as often?
Did you let yourself enjoy it, or did you take something off it afterwards?
Review questions
Is the balance between fast and slow moving in the right direction?
Is there anything in your week now that you look forward to?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
At least two of your three weekly steps are the slow kind.
You would be comfortable with anybody knowing about everything on your list.
You have written both warnings, the flatness one and the escalation one.
Your second response is faster and less negotiable than your first.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: Knowledge means feeling informed and understanding what is going on, whether that is about your own case, your own health, a decision that affects you, or simply how something works. It takes enough information to stop you guessing, and no cleverness.

This need does not announce itself the way hunger or loneliness do. It shows up sideways, as suspicion, as resentment, or as a flat refusal to ask a question you need answered because asking feels like admitting you do not already know. Left unmet for long enough, not knowing starts to feel like being deliberately kept out, whether or not that is true.

Feeling informed means understanding the things that affect your life, from people and sources you can check. Opinions about things, or a great deal of information from any source that will provide it, do not make you informed.
Signs of progress
When you do not understand something that affects you, you ask the person who knows.
You know roughly where you stand on your obligations, your finances and your health.
You can tell what you have checked from what you have only heard.
Not knowing something makes you curious.
You are comfortable saying “I don’t know, I will find out” out loud.
Signs of drifting
You avoid asking questions because asking feels like exposing a gap.
You assume the worst about a situation because nobody has told you anything, and the silence fills with suspicion.
You have stopped opening letters, checking accounts, or asking about your own situation because not knowing feels safer than knowing.
You have strong opinions about things you have never checked.
You feel like everyone else is working from information you were never given.
Why this need matters

Feeling permanently kept in the dark, about your own case, your own supervision, your own family’s decisions, tends to push a person one of two ways, and neither helps. One is to stop asking altogether and disengage. The other is to go looking for answers in whatever source will give one, checked or not, private or not. Either way you end up running your life on guesswork and private theories with nothing checked, and a life like that is easier to justify to yourself in secret. Understanding your own situation, including your own patterns and your own risk, connects directly to Concept 18 of Understanding My Past, Understanding My Risk Factors. Use that understanding here.
Some ask what you already know, some ask what stops you finding out the rest.
1. Rate your ability
Do not guess this one from memory. Ask somebody a direct question first, then rate yourself against what they tell you.
Ask the person who knows

Pick one thing that affects you right now that you are not entirely sure about, a condition of your supervision, a fact about your case, a decision somebody else made about you. Ask the person who knows. Then answer these.
What did you think the answer was, before you asked?
What was the answer?
Rate this need overall
Rate Knowledge today, 0 to 10, where 0 means you are mostly guessing about the things that matter and 10 means you generally know where you stand and check what you do not.
If the gap between your guess and the actual answer was large, it usually means you have been avoiding the asking and could have understood the answer.
2. Why this matters to me
Below is a bank of words for how it feels to be kept in the dark. Pick the two or three that fit you, then check your answer against the test underneath.
Suspicious. Small. Foolish. Excluded. Behind. Anxious. Resentful. Written off. Managed rather than told. Safer not knowing.
Check your words
a.	Have you described an actual situation, not just the general feeling?
b.	Have you said what you did in response as well as how you felt?

blocks.x: Creativity means making things, expressing yourself and doing it your own way, with somewhere legitimate to put your own stamp on something, whether that is building, fixing, cooking, drawing, writing, music, growing things, or any other way of making.

You may hear “creativity” and assume it does not apply to you because you do not paint or play an instrument. That reading is too narrow. The need is about making something that did not exist before and that has some part of you in it. It also covers having at least one part of your life where you set the terms yourself.
Unmet, this need shows up as a flatness, a sense that every part of your day is either work or waiting, with nowhere that is yours.
Signs of progress
At least one thing in your week involves making or building something.
You have a way of doing at least one everyday thing that is recognisably yours.
Finishing something you made gives you a satisfaction that other things do not.
You are willing to be bad at something new for a while and put getting better ahead of looking competent.
Some part of your week is not dictated by anybody else’s rules.
Signs of drifting
Every hour of your week is either obligation or passive time, spent watching or scrolling.
You cannot remember the last time you finished making something.
You used to make things and stopped, and you have stopped noticing that you stopped.
Nothing in your life feels like it has your own stamp on it.
You avoid starting anything new because you do not want to be bad at it in front of anyone, including yourself.
Why this need matters

A life with no legitimate outlet for making or expressing anything tends to narrow to whatever is left. Check whether the narrowing happened around online behaviour that eventually became offending. The space was private, it was yours, and it was the one place you felt any control or mastery at all. This need is not a substitute explanation for offending, and it may not be true for you. Where it is true, rebuilding a legitimate space that is yours, where you make things and set your own terms, removes some of the pull that a private, ungoverned space once had.

What changed around then that took it away?

If someone took away every screen in your house for a month, what would you do with your hands?

blocks.x: Community means belonging to something bigger than yourself, in a place, group or role where you are counted in. Close relationships get their own section later, and this need covers the wider sense of fitting somewhere.

Belonging is different from being around people. A man can be surrounded by people all day at work and still have nowhere he belongs, and a man who lives alone can belong solidly to a club, a church, a team, or a street. The question is whether there is a “we” anywhere in your life that you are part of.

Losing this need rarely feels like a single event. Usually it is a slow drift, missing a few things, feeling slightly more like a visitor each time, until you have stopped going altogether and barely noticed the last time you did.
Signs of progress
You have at least one group, place, or activity where people would notice if you stopped turning up.
You feel like a participant somewhere, someone more than a name on a list.
You could ask somebody in that group for a favour without it feeling strange.
At least one group of people has some idea what is going on in your life.
Being part of something does not depend entirely on one other person.
Signs of drifting
You cannot name a single group or place where somebody would notice your absence.
You have stopped going to things you used to be part of, and nobody has chased you about it.
Whenever you are in a group, you feel like you are watching it from outside.
All of your sense of belonging runs through one relationship, and if that person is unavailable you have nowhere.
You assume any group would rather you were not there, without having tested that assumption recently.
Why this need matters

Isolation from any ordinary, positive group can be part of the pattern behind offending. Being alone does not cause it directly. A person with nowhere he belongs has nobody around him who would notice a slide, and nowhere that pulls him back toward an ordinary life when things get hard. Rebuilding some form of belonging, a group, a role, a regular place, puts ordinary people back in a position to notice, and gives you somewhere to be pulled back towards.

Rate yourself, then rate yourself as somebody who has known you a long time would rate you. This need is often judged differently from the outside than from within.

A lower self-rating than the other person’s guess often means you feel like an outsider somewhere that would count you in. A higher one often means you are counting a group you have already drifted away from.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?

Is there somewhere you already half-belong that you could go back to?

blocks.x: This need is about having a say in your own life and making your own decisions, from the everyday ones up: what you eat, how you spend an evening, what you spend money on. Without it, everything feels decided for you or around you.

You may be constrained in some of this need right now, by supervision conditions, reporting obligations, or decisions other people have had to make. Those constraints are real, and nothing here works out how to get around them. This section covers the space they leave and how much of it you use.

Feeling that you have no say anywhere in your life wears you down over time, whatever the reason. Pushing against the constraints that are there does not fix that. Notice and use the choices that still exist, and there are usually more of them than a powerless feeling lets you see.
Signs of progress
You make decisions, including the little ones.
You know the difference between a constraint that exists and one you have assumed without checking.
You can say what you think, to the people it is appropriate to say it to, without it feeling dangerous.
You have at least a few areas of your life where the decision is up to you.
A condition or an obligation does not feel like having no life of your own at all.
Signs of drifting
You feel like everything in your life is decided by somebody else, all the time, in every area.
You have stopped making even the everyday decisions that are up to you.
You assume a restriction applies more broadly than it does, and have never checked.
You feel resentful most of the time, without necessarily being able to say at what.
You have started testing rules in ways nobody sees, to feel you still have some control.
Why this need matters

A man who feels he has no legitimate say anywhere in his life is at risk of taking back a sense of control somewhere illegitimate. Examples are testing a rule, keeping a secret, or doing something because nobody said he could not. The pattern comes from the powerless feeling. Pushing back against lawful constraints does not fix it. Finding and using the choices that remain does, and the feeling of having no say stops being accurate.

What would you tell him to stop assuming he cannot do, without checking?
What would you warn him against, if he started trying to claw back control in the wrong places?

blocks.x: This need is about being good at what you do, mastering something, and getting better at it over time. It does not have to be paid employment. Volunteering, study, running a household properly, or a serious hobby can all meet it, though paid work may supply much of it for you.

Mastery gives you a skill you can point to, in place of a vague sense of being adequate or not. It also provides one of the steadiest sources of daily structure a life can have, and unstructured time is where other problems tend to grow.

Mastery can go unmet in two ways that look similar from the outside. One is having no work or role at all. The other is having one but never getting better at it, going through the motions without building skill or pride.

You have a role, paid or not, that gives structure to your day or week.
You have a skill you could point to.
You are still getting better at something.
The work itself gives you something, as well as the outcome or the pay at the end of it.
You would be comfortable describing what you do to somebody who asked.
Signs of drifting
Your days have no structure, and one blends into the next.
You cannot think of anything you are good at, only things you get by on.
You have not improved at anything in longer than you can comfortably say.
Work, if you have it, is endured and gives you nothing back.
You avoid describing what you do, and you do not think much of it yourself.
Why this need matters

Unstructured time and a flat sense of being no good at anything in particular are both well-established factors in offending. Idleness does not cause harm directly. An unstructured day leaves far more room for private, ungoverned time, and a low sense of competence anywhere legitimate can make a private source of mastery or control, however unhealthy, feel more important than it should. Rebuilding structure and a checkable sense of being good at something reduces both pressures.
Some ask what you are good at, some ask what has stopped you using it.
1. Rate your ability
Rate how competent you feel at something, then rate how much you use that competence day to day. Having a skill and using it are different things.
Rate how competent you feel at the thing you are best at, 0 to 10.
Rate how much of your week involves using that skill, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ
A skill you rate highly but rarely use is sitting idle for a reason, and the reason tells you more than the skill does.
If you rate a skill highly but rarely use it, write it here, with what keeps it out of your week.
2. Why this matters to me
Below is a bank of words people use for how it feels to have no structure or sense of mastery. Pick the two or three that fit, then check your answer against the test underneath.
Adrift. Adequate at best. Wasted. Restless. Bored. Purposeless. Going through the motions. Behind where I should be. Unused.
Check your words
a.	Have you written a role, task or skill, as well as the general feeling?
b.	Have you said what a normal day currently looks like, structured or not?
c.	Have you said whether the gap is about having no role, or having one you are not improving at?
d.	Would somebody reading this know what you want more competence or structure in?
Why does Work matter to you? Say what you want more competence in.
3. This need and my offending
Write about the sense of competence, mastery or structure the behaviour gave you, and what an unstructured or purposeless stretch of time had left open. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
The stretch of time this happened in was one where my days looked like __________.
What the behaviour gave me that felt like skill or mastery was __________.
If my days had structure and something I was building competence at, I think __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Work need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.
Write down both the unstructured time and the absent sense of mastery. A general resolve to “get busier” does not tell you what to change. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to build structure and growing competence.
Pick one thing to improve
Paid work, a trade skill, study, or running your household properly all count.
Attach a repeated action
Not “get better at my job”. “Ask my supervisor on Monday to show me the part of the job I have never been trained on.”
Check your answer
a.	It gives one skill or role.
b.	It has a day and an action attached.
c.	It is a change you would notice in yourself within a week.
Write two or three steps for Work, each one a change you would notice in yourself within a week.
5. Signs of success
Progress here shows up as structure and competence you can point to, and those are easier to check than a feeling.
What would somebody else notice
Somebody who works with you or sees your week. What would they notice about your days having more structure?
What would you be able to do now that you could not do six months ago?
What would they say if asked whether you are good at what you do?
6. Signs of concern
These are early, before unstructured time has become the norm again.
Trace back an unstructured stretch
Think of a period when your days had little shape and you were not building anything. Go back through it until you reach the first sign.
Once your days had clearly lost their structure, what did a typical one look like?
What was the first routine or task you stopped doing?
If you can say what that first dropped routine was, see your psychologist about it this week. If you cannot see them this week, write the date you noticed it and review it then.
7. Response to concern
Write a response for each situation.
Build both as if-then
If I notice a week has gone by with no structure to my days, then I will __________ before the next one starts.
If I notice I have stopped trying to improve at anything at all, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not following through is __________, and my answer to it is __________.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Work? Write the excuse you are most likely to use, and your answer to it.
8. Progress, changes and support
Build on what worked
Write one thing you got better at in the last month.
What made that possible, and could you use that approach again?
Review questions
Do your days have more structure than they did last time?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps is an actual skill or role, with a day and action attached.
You could start at least one of those steps this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

examples.why: Monday is the day and the supervisor is the person to ask, so it does not wait on something happening by itself. The forklift ticket is a skill, where “upskill” would be a direction.
