blocks.x: Relationships means closeness with the people who matter to you, and having at least one adult relationship in your life with closeness in it, somebody who knows the truth about how you are, as well as how you present.

This section covers adult relationships only: a partner, family members, friends. Do not use it to work through anything to do with contact with children, including your own. Any question about contact with a child is governed by legal orders, case workers and the professionals involved in each decision, and this section does not touch it. If that is unresolved for you, take it to your caseworker or your psychologist, or to Legal Aid or a family lawyer in your state or territory. Do not work it out alone.

Closeness differs from having people around. You may have family nearby, or a partner in the house, and still have nobody who knows what is going on with you. Depth in at least one relationship meets this need.
Signs of progress
At least one adult knows something true and current about how you are.
You can be disagreed with by somebody close to you without the relationship feeling at risk.
You ask how somebody else is doing and wait for the answer.
You would tell at least one person if things were going badly.
Closeness with someone does not depend entirely on them not knowing something important about you.
Signs of drifting
Everybody in your life gets a managed, edited version of you, and nobody gets the rest.
You cannot think of anybody you would tell if things were going badly.
Conversations with people close to you stay on the surface, weather, logistics, nothing underneath.
You assume that if people knew you, they would not want to be close to you.
Being around people and being close to somebody feel alike, and you have stopped noticing the difference.
Why this need matters

Isolation from adult closeness is one of the better-established patterns behind offending, and it has two effects. It removes the people most likely to notice a slide early, and it can leave a private, unmet need for closeness looking for somewhere else to be met, sometimes somewhere it should never have gone. Rebuilding closeness with an adult who knows the true version of you gives you a legitimate place to meet this need and puts somebody in a position to notice if things start to go wrong.
Some ask who already knows the true version of you, some ask what stops you letting them.
1. Rate your ability
Rate yourself, then have a go at rating yourself as the person closest to you would. You may be surprised by the gap.
Rate Relationships as you see it today, 0 to 10.
Rate how close you are as the adult closest to you would rate it, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ
A higher self-rating than theirs usually means you are counting proximity as closeness. A lower one usually means you do not give the relationship credit for what it provides.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Look at it from a few angles. Pick the two or three you have most to say about.
Questions to think about
Who, if anyone, currently knows something true and current about how you are?
What is the cost, over time, of the edited version of you that other people get?
Is there a relationship in your life that has room for more honesty than it has now, if you let it?
What would it mean to you to be known by one other adult, instead of managed by everyone?
3. This need and my offending
Write about the closeness or connection you were missing in your adult relationships, and what that absence felt like. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
The closeness I was missing in my adult relationships at the time was __________.
The person I could have gone to instead, but did not, was __________, and the reason I did not was __________.
If I had let one adult see the true version of me at the time, I think __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Relationships need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.
An unmet need for closeness usually feels like something vaguer. Write it here, and say with whom. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to bring more honesty into one existing adult relationship.
Pick one adult relationship
A partner, a family member, or a friend. Somewhere the raw material for closeness already exists, even if it is not being used.
Pick one thing to share
Not “be more open with my family”. “Tell my brother on Sunday that this year has been harder than I have been letting on.”
Check your answer
a.	It gives one person’s name, and “my family” does not count.
b.	It states something true you would say.
c.	It has a day attached.
Write two or three steps for Relationships, each one with a day attached.
5. Signs of success
Progress here shows up as a conversation, and a conversation is easier to check than a feeling of closeness.
What would somebody else notice
The person you put in box four. What would they notice had changed about how much you tell them?
What would they say if asked whether they feel like they know the person you are?
What would you have told them, that you would not have told them a year ago?
6. Signs of concern
These are early, before the edited version of you has become the only version anybody gets.
Trace back a closed-off time
Think of a period when you were managing everybody and telling nobody the truth. Work backwards and find the first sign.
Once you had clearly closed off, what did your conversations with people close to you look like?
What was the first true thing you stopped saying, that made the rest easier to stop saying too?
If you could say what that first thing was, do not leave it until your next review. Mention it to your psychologist this week, or write the date you noticed it and review it then.
7. Response to concern
Write a response for each of the two different situations here.
Build both as if-then
If I notice I have gone back to giving everybody the managed version, then I will __________ within __________.
If I notice I am carrying something I have told nobody, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not following through is __________, and my answer to it is __________.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Relationships? Write the excuse you are most likely to use for not following through, and your answer to it.
8. Progress, changes and support
Build on what worked
Write one conversation from the last month in which you told the truth and that you would not have had a year ago.
What made that possible, and could you use that approach again?
Review questions
Does at least one person currently know the true version of you?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps gives one adult, with a day attached.
You could start at least one of those steps this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name.
Nothing you have written touches on contact with a child in any way. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: The introduction set out four ways a plan goes wrong: a harmful route, a plan that is too narrow, goals that fight each other, and steps you do not yet have enough to work with. Use this page to find them in your own plan. Come back to this page after Relationships, once you have something written in every one of the eleven need sections.
Reading all box 4 answers

Before you check for any particular fault, open every need section and read only the box 4 answers, the steps, one after another, without stopping to read anything else. Reading eleven steps side by side shows up things you cannot see when you read them one section at a time, weeks apart.
Fault one: harmful route
A step can meet a need and still be the wrong step, either because it puts you somewhere you have no business being or because meeting the need this way would hurt somebody else.
Does any step involve children in a way your legal conditions or your safety plan do not allow, or seek out new contact with children, such as supervising, coaching or minding?
Does any step depend on nobody else knowing what you are doing?
Would you be comfortable reading every one of your eleven sets of steps aloud to your psychologist, or to the person you chose in “sharing your plan”?
Does any step rely on you being alone with somebody who could not consent to what you are asking of them, or on a situation you have engineered rather than one that arose naturally?
Fault two: too narrow
A plan that depends heavily on two or three needs and leaves the rest nearly empty holds up until something knocks out one of those two or three, and then the plan has no other support.
Which need sections have little or nothing written in box 4? Go and look at the pages.
If you imagine losing your two strongest needs tomorrow, a job ending or a relationship breaking down, is there anything left in the other nine that would hold you up?
Are three or more of your eleven steps one step written in different words, for example “spend more time with family” appearing under three different needs?
Fault three: conflicting goals
Two goals can both be good and still be impossible to have at once. If you have not decided in advance which one gives way, life will decide for you, usually at the worst moment.
List all eleven of your box 4 steps in one place. Do any two of them need the same hours of the same day?
Does meeting one need on your list undercut another, for example a work step that leaves no time or energy for the relationships or play steps?
If two steps did collide in a given week, have you decided which one wins, or would you be deciding that for the first time under pressure?
Fault four: missing resources
A step can be a good step and still fail because it needs a skill, some money, transport, a licence or an opportunity that you do not currently have.
Is any step waiting on money you do not currently have spare?
Does any step depend on a skill, a licence or a piece of equipment you do not yet have, with no earlier step written in to get it?
Does any step need somebody else’s permission or availability, with no plan for what happens if they say no or are not around?
A gap like this means the goal is missing its own first step. Add that step and keep the goal.
If this check changes something
Go back into the relevant need section and change the box 4 answer directly. You do not need to explain the change anywhere. Finding a fault here means the check worked.
Removing a step from the page leaves whatever caused it in place.

blocks.x: A psychologist or the person you are sharing your plan with is not the one living with the plan day to day, and may see a collision or a gap that you cannot. Ask somebody to look at this page alongside your eleven sets of answers, and that is what “who you will share your plan with” is for.

A handful of words in this workbook come from research or from the SafeCare model. Here is what each one means. Tapping a linked word anywhere in the workbook brings you straight to its entry here, and each entry has a link back to where you were.
What each word means here
Fundamental needs

The handful of basic, ordinary things every person is chasing: feeling well, feeling calm, feeling close to somebody, feeling like they are good at something, and feeling like their life adds up to something. Nobody has to be taught to want any of these, and wanting them was never the problem. This workbook works through eleven of them, one section each. A Good Lives Model term.
Pseudo Adult
One of three parts of a person described in the SafeCare model. The grown-up front you learned to put on, the face the world sees. See also Inner Child and True Adult.
Inner Child

One of three parts of a person described in the SafeCare model. The part of you that got stuck at the age when something happened that you could not handle. It does not go anywhere and is not meant to. It is not a stage you get past or something to be got rid of. See also Pseudo Adult and True Adult.
True Adult

One of three parts of a person described in the SafeCare model. The grown-up child, made up of all three parts, and its job is to act as the umpire between the other two. An umpire needs two sides on the field. The True Adult listens to the Pseudo Adult, listens to the Inner Child, and decides. It does not silence either of them, and it never stops having the job.
Approach goals

Things you are going to do as well as things you are going to stop doing. A plan made only of rules about what to avoid is not yet a life, and this workbook asks for approach goals throughout. A Good Lives Model term.

blocks.x: This is a short form for checking in on your eleven needs once you have done the full workbook at least once, whether that was last month or years ago.
What this is for

You do not need to reopen and rework all eleven full sections every time you want to check how things are going. In a few minutes you can rate your eleven needs, compare them with last time, and write a short list of actions.
This does not replace the full sections. If a number has dropped a long way, or something in these few minutes worries you, go back and spend time in that need’s full section.
This is the short version of the review process already described in the introduction. See Your review dates
Before you fill this in

blocks.x: Purpose

This guide sets out how to run or support Planning My Future, the eleven-need workbook this library is built around. The register is professional, written for a facilitator, but nothing in it is restricted from anyone who reads it. If you are working through the plan yourself, most of this will read as background, and that is fine. Read the sections on the safety boundary and on the four faults either way.

How to Use This Workbook explains the eight-box structure directly to the person working through it, and this guide assumes you have read it. This guide covers what a facilitator needs to do around that structure.
How the workbook is built

Eleven fundamental needs, each with the eight-box structure, in a fixed order that runs from more concrete needs to ones that take more thinking. Life opens the sequence and Relationships closes it deliberately, and the closer needs benefit from everything the person has already worked through. Each need’s example page dissects weak answers and supplies no model to copy, following the library’s example-page pattern, so do not treat it as a template.
Box 3 in every section, “This need and my offending”, changes the plan more than almost any other box. It is also the one box with a hard safety boundary built into it.
Box 3 safety boundary

Every box 3 asks for feeling and motivation, never method. The instruction on the page already tells the group member this and tells them to stop and raise it with you if their answer starts heading into method. You are the person they raise it with.

blocks.head: Redirecting a box 3 answer
blocks.x: Stop the writing there. Do not let the account continue to a natural end out of politeness. Acknowledge the feeling part of what they wrote, since that part was the task and is often the hardest to say out loud. Then explain that the written plan may be read by others and that describing method in it is not what any box in this workbook asks for. What comes next is a conversation with you, and no further writing. Checking Your Plan uses the same escalation wording for the harmful-route fault. Use that wording in the moment, so group members hear one consistent message across the workbook.

Expect this to come up, and plan for it before the first session where box 3 is reached. Know in advance who a group member is referred to if the conversation brings up something beyond what this workbook or this group is set up to deal with.
Pacing a group through it
This workbook has no session-by-session mapping, unlike the SafeCare concept series, and the following is a starting structure, not a fixed curriculum.
Open with the introduction and how-to-use sections in a single session, since both are short and the workbook does not make sense without them.

One need per session is a reasonable default pace. Shorter or more straightforward needs can be paired in a single session if the pace is going well; do not pair two needs if either produced a difficult box 3 disclosure in earlier work.
Build in time in each session for box 3. Sessions run long there and should be allowed to.

Individualise every plan. The prompts, word banks and sentence stems are a scaffold. An answer that closely matches somebody else’s or an example page is a sign to slow down, not a sign of a session going well.
Supporting faults and review

Once a person has something in box 4 for every need, the four faults check tests the plan as a set for a harmful route, being too narrow, goals that fight each other, or not enough to work with. The first time, walk through it together, as a harmful route in a person’s own plan is easier to miss from the inside.

The review process, and the shorter My Review tool built for repeated solo use afterward, both depend on the person having somebody to share the plan with. Help them choose that person deliberately during the sharing section, and follow up on whether the conversation with that person took place.
Low literacy or no facilitator

For lower reading levels, read sections aloud, allow spoken answers to be written down by whoever is supporting, and use the worked examples to show the level of detail being asked for, not the content. Short answers are the standard everywhere in this workbook, and a shorter answer should not read as the workbook not working for him.

The workbook itself is written to work with nobody present at all, years after any group has ended. If you are supporting somebody using it that way, everything above about box 3 and the four faults still applies. It means you are the one person they have.
Scope note: fidelity monitoring

This guide does not include a GLM fidelity monitoring tool or a session-by-session fidelity checklist. For that material, use Prescott, Willis and Ward’s GLM Fidelity Monitoring Tool. Do not read this guide as a fidelity instrument.
Cautions
This workbook is not a risk assessment and does not replace one. Continue to use whatever validated tool and structured professional judgement process your service already applies.

Be clear with the people you support at the outset about the limits of confidentiality and any mandatory reporting duties that apply in your jurisdiction, in the same terms the introduction already sets out to them directly.

The approach-goal model this workbook uses is based on evidence that traditional, avoidance-only relapse prevention worksheets do not reduce reoffending (see References). That evidence is about worksheet design and does not mean any person’s risk is low. Do not let this workbook’s tone soften how you communicate risk elsewhere.
Purpose

This brief sets out the approach for the relapse prevention component: two plans, one for online child exploitation material offending and one for contact offending. Two further components sit alongside either plan, on reporting obligations and on prepared disclosure. The register is professional, written for a facilitator, but nothing in it is restricted from a reader. If you are the person completing a plan rather than running one, the next three sections explain the thinking behind it. The sections after that are written for whoever is guiding you, and you can read them too.
How this plan differs

The classic relapse prevention worksheet asks a person to list high-risk situations, warning signs and coping responses, then to avoid the situations. The strongest test of that model, the SOTEP randomised trial, found no reduction in sexual or violent reoffending compared with untreated controls. The men who reoffended less were those who met the goals of treatment.

The program materials in this project reflect this. They replace the traditional relapse prevention plan with an integrated good life, self-regulation and risk-management plan. The centre of the plan is the approach goals, the life the person is building, and risk factors are treated as obstacles to that life. Approach-focused work also improves engagement and disclosure of lapses, which helps in a group with mixed motivation and mixed reading ability.
The model in short

The plan is built on the good life the reader wants and the healthy ways of reaching it. Early warning signs and a getting-back-on-track section are kept because they are concrete and useful, and they sit inside the approach-goal structure. The aim is a life that is incompatible with offending, which asks for more than avoiding offending.
Why two separate versions
Online and contact offending follow different pathways, so the two plans differ in their risk sections and share one overall structure.
Online child exploitation material version
Centres on problematic internet use, the emotional function of viewing, escalation and collecting patterns, and structured, monitored device use.
Gives extra attention to victim awareness, because the absence of a visible victim can feed the belief that no one was harmed.
Avoids a plan built on total internet abstinence, which cannot work when work, banking and daily life run through one device.
Contact version
Centres on situations involving access to children, planning ahead, transparency with trusted adults, and supervision conditions.
Treats being alone with a child as a situation to plan around, as part of the wider good-life goals.
Two further components
Living With My Obligations and What I Tell People are separate from either plan. Both work for a reader working alone, as the rest of this component does.

Living With My Obligations treats reporting and supervision duties as a planning constraint. It states in its own text that it is not legal advice and shows the date it was written. It tells the reader to check the current consolidation of the Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004 and to raise anything about his own situation with the police or a lawyer. Do not add to it or answer questions from it as though you were qualified to give legal advice, whatever your own familiarity with the Act.

What I Tell People prepares a disclosure at three levels, one line, a short version, and a full version, plus what to do if someone already knows or if telling somebody goes badly. The two drafts to watch for are a denial and an over-disclosure that goes into detail. The example page in that document takes one of each apart. Your job in the room is the one described there, to help him settle on an accurate, brief account that does not grovel, hide the offence or rehearse it.
Running it in the group
The running notes below are for a facilitator and can be skipped if you are working through this yourself. Read the cautions and key resources further down either way.
Build the good life and support sections first. Do not open with the offence or the risk list.
Individualise every plan, using the prompts as a scaffold.
For lower reading levels, read prompts aloud, allow spoken answers to be written down for the person, and use the worked examples as a model.
Treat the plan as a living document. Review and update it as the person changes.
Cautions
The plan is not a risk assessment. Use a validated tool such as the CPORT for online offenders alongside structured professional judgement.
Contact reoffending rates among online-only offenders are low. Do not pitch the plan in a way that overstates contact risk to that group.
No program has yet proven a recidivism reduction for online offenders, so this component is evidence-informed rather than evidence-based.
Integrate supervision and reporting duties under the Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004 where they apply.
Be clear at the outset about the limits of confidentiality and any mandatory reporting duties.
Key resources
Yates and Prescott, Building a Better Life, and the clinician guide Applying the Good Lives and Self-Regulation Models.
i-SOTP and Inform Plus materials on online offending.
Take your time with this short guide to the plan you are going to build.
What the plan is

Your staying-on-track plan does two things at once. One is about the life you want to live, the other about keeping yourself and other people safe. The two belong together, and when your life is going well, staying safe gets easier.
What the plan aims for

You may be expecting a plan full of rules that all start with the word “don’t”. That kind of plan is hard to stick to, and it does not give you much to aim for. Your plan will have a few things to watch out for, but most of it is about what you are building and where you are heading.
Your good life

We start with what you care about. That might be family, friendship, feeling at home, doing good work, learning something, or having some peace of mind. The plan looks at healthy ways to reach them that do not cause harm.
Spotting when you are drifting

Rough patches come up. The plan helps you notice the early signs that you are slipping off track, such as feeling low, cutting yourself off from people, or using a screen to escape. Noticing these early gives you time to act.
If you have a slip
If you have a slip, you can pick up from where you are. Your plan lists steps to take and people you can call. Reaching out early is a strength.
Building it in a group

Build the plan one part at a time. You do not need to be a strong reader. The prompts can be read out loud, and a psychologist or someone you trust can write your answers down for you. Update the plan as things change. If you meet regularly with a psychologist, bring this with you to each session.
Building it on your own

You might be building this plan years after a programme has finished, with nobody looking over your shoulder. Work through it at whatever pace suits you, in whatever order makes sense. Return later to any part you are not ready for. If reading or writing is hard going, use whatever your phone or computer offers for reading text aloud, or talk your answers into a voice recorder and type them up after. It can help to show what you have written to a psychologist or somebody else you trust, but the plan works without anyone.

blocks.x: The plan asks a person to work through positions in an offence cycle. The first is a build-up (the situation, the thoughts, and the feelings that preceded an offence). blocks.head: Differences from the current plan
blocks.x: The Relapse Prevention Plan built for this library uses a different model, an integrated Good Lives and self-regulation plan built around approach goals (see the Facilitator Brief in Relapse Prevention Plan). That choice rests on the SOTEP randomised trial, which found no reduction in reoffending among men who completed a traditional relapse prevention plan of this kind, compared with untreated controls. This chapter is not a proposal to revert to the earlier model. It keeps the instrument that influenced this programme’s history available to a clinician working with someone who completed it, or comparing the two approaches.
The positions in the cycle
Build-up: situation

The events and circumstances in a person’s life in the lead-up to an offence: relationship strain, financial pressure, isolation, conflict at work, loss, and similar. This position asks what was happening, before it asks what a person felt about it.
Build-up: thoughts
The beliefs and attitudes held about those events before offending, the private case a person was making to himself for why his situation justified what came next.
Build-up: feelings
The emotional state in the period before an offence, both the acute feeling immediately before it and any longer-running mood that had been present for some time.
Acting out: thoughts and feelings

The internal experience during an offence itself: the thoughts that occurred once the decision to offend had effectively already been made, and any shift in feeling from that point of decision through to the end of the act. Consistent with every other worksheet in this library, this position describes internal experience only, never conduct.
Afterward: feelings
The physical and emotional aftermath: relief, shame, confidence, or another feeling entirely, and what, if anything, the behaviour appeared to deliver emotionally in the short term.
Afterward: justifying thoughts
The denial, minimisation or justification used afterward to make the behaviour easier to live with, the account a person gave himself, distinct from any account he may have given anyone else.
Step-offs: strategies

Practical actions intended to interrupt the cycle at whichever position they can be applied to. The original instrument’s own worked example was moving a household computer into a shared family space, a concrete, checkable action.
Using this in a session

A facilitator or clinician working with someone who completed this earlier plan can use it as a point of comparison. The useful questions are where the offence-cycle model called attention to something the approach-goal model does not ask about directly, and where the reverse happened. See the Facilitator Brief in Relapse Prevention Plan for the reasoning behind the plan’s current model, and My Plan (online version and contact version), also in Relapse Prevention Plan, for what a person completes now.

If you are the person who completed this earlier plan yourself, this chapter describes your own record. You can use it as a point of comparison too, noticing where the old build-up, acting out, afterward and step-offs questions asked about something your current plan does not, and where your current plan asks about something this one never did.

blocks.x: This chapter is Part B of A Clinician’s Framework, which covers practices that existed but are not something to do today. It describes how SafeCare screened and assessed a person before treatment began, during the programme’s operating years. No facilitator can run it today, and no current version of it exists to opt into or request. It stays here so a clinician working with someone who went through it, or comparing it with current practice, is not working from a gap.

Before intake proper, a caller went through a pre-intake conversation, still anonymous at that stage, that let a person ask questions and hear enough about what the programme involved before committing to it formally.
What intake gathered
At intake, the programme gathered as much history as it reasonably could, which informed treatment and gave a benchmark to measure progress against as treatment went on.
The genogram
Drawing a family genogram was a standard part of intake, described in full in Understanding My Past, Concept 7, Your Family Map.
The structured interview

A structured interview covered a person’s history broadly. It asked about drug and alcohol use, mental and physical health, any history of abuse, neglect or violence they had experienced themselves, criminal history, and education and work. It also covered a general psychological profile and a history of the offending itself.
The assessment battery

Alongside the interview, intake included a set of formal tests, standardised and scored the same way for everyone who takes them. Each is described here by what it was and roughly how long it took, with no account of what a particular answer meant, consistent with how this library treats every such instrument it mentions.
A personality test, around ninety minutes.
A psycho-sexual inventory, around ninety minutes.
An empathy test, around twenty minutes.
A sexual fantasy test, around fifteen minutes.
A questionnaire about attitudes to children and sexuality, around fifteen minutes.

None of these instruments, or their items, are reproduced anywhere in this library. What each measured in general terms (personality, sexual interest patterns, empathy, fantasy content and attitudes) is stated so a clinician knows what intake covered. Nothing here would let anyone administer or score them.
Using this in a session

A facilitator or clinician working with someone who went through this earlier process can use it as background. It describes what intake used to involve, and nothing in this chapter authorises reinstating any part of it.

If you are the person who went through this yourself, this chapter describes your own intake. Reading it back lets you check which parts of it still apply to you and what your current plan and worksheets ask about instead.

blocks.head: About this chapter
blocks.x: This chapter is Part A of A Clinician’s Framework, which covers claims to be checked against research. It states a theory and explains why it has no evidentiary weight. It does not describe what happened to you or what you are likely to do, and it is not a way of assessing anyone you support. If your own history matches the pattern described below, that alone tells you nothing reliable about yourself or anyone else. Understanding My Past, Concept 9, Patterns: Age, Gender and Form, treats this ground the same way, as a fact to state and never as an explanation to use.
What the theory claims

Gender of Offender Theory holds that a person abused by an offender of the same gender is more likely to go on to offend themselves, while a person abused by an offender of the opposite gender is more likely to experience further victimisation and its long-term effects. The theory is Christabel Chamarette’s own clinical theory, drawn from her observations over SafeCare’s operating years. It has not been peer-reviewed (checked by other researchers before publication) or published. It has not been tested against a comparison group either (a matched group of people without that abuse history, tracked as the abused group was, to see whether the pattern holds up).
Why the reasoning is omitted

The theory’s own reasoning links a person’s later risk to their childhood abuser’s gender in a way that works, in practice, as an explanation for offending rather than an account of it. Concept 9 of Understanding My Past found that this same reasoning does the same thing whichever direction it runs, so reaching for it is usually an excuse, not an accurate account. That finding does not change because the reader of this chapter may be a facilitator rather than the person the pattern describes. A Clinician’s Framework has no separate, more permissive readership, so the reasoning is not set out here either.
The published evidence

One piece of verifiable, published research addresses the general pattern, independent of any theory about gender: Ogloff, Cutajar, Mann and Mullen’s 2012 forty-five year follow-up study, cited in the same chapter of the book. Of male victims of childhood sexual abuse in that study, 5% were later convicted of a sexual offence, rising to 9.2% among those abused at age twelve or older, against 0.6% of a non-abused comparison group. The study is cited here instead of Gender of Offender Theory’s own reasoning, consistent with the rule that the SafeCare book is the authority unless a verifiable published source says otherwise. For anything stated as evidence, this chapter relies on a verifiable published source, not the book’s unpublished theory.
Using this in a session

A facilitator who hears a client use this theory to explain his own abuse history can say what this chapter says, that the reasoning has not been shown to predict anything reliably and using it is usually an excuse. The client’s own Concept 9 worksheet, Patterns: Age, Gender and Form, already asks him to state the fact and leave the theory alone. This chapter gives the facilitator that discipline in professional language.

If you are reading this on your own, you can apply that discipline in your own Concept 9 worksheet. If your history matches the pattern described above, write it there as a fact and leave it, as that worksheet asks. You do not need anybody in the room to apply it.

blocks.head: About this chapter
blocks.x: This chapter sits outside Part A, Part B and Part C of A Clinician’s Framework. It is the caveat the preamble refers to when it cites Willis and Grace’s finding that better release planning tracked lower sexual recidivism. The preamble gives that finding with a short qualification and sends a treating professional here for the rest. Both consolidated reference documents do the same, in identical wording.
What the research shows
What the two studies measured

Willis and Grace built a coding protocol, a fixed scoring guide applied to every file in the same manner. It scored the quality of release planning for men leaving two New Zealand prison-based treatment programmes for child molesters, Kia Marama in the 2008 study and Te Piriti in the 2009 study. Each was compared against a matched group who did not go on to reoffend. The protocol scored only the reintegration report a treatment coordinator prepared for the Parole Board or Community Probation Service ahead of release, and never anything the men themselves wrote. It rated accommodation planning, social support planning, employment planning, and either Good Lives Model secondary goods (the everyday goals through which a person’s deeper needs are expressed) in the 2008 study, or documented idiosyncratic risk factors (warning signs particular to that person) in the 2009 study. A separate item recorded the man’s motivation to follow through with the plan, and that item was the treating therapist’s own rating of him, not a self-report.
Correlation and causation

Correlational means two things move together without one being shown to produce the other, as against causal, where one has been shown to bring about the other. Both studies compared existing groups after the fact, with no random assignment of planning quality, so neither can tell whether better planning caused the better outcome or only tracked something else that produced both. The 2008 study tested this directly. When IQ and a psychometric measure of dynamic risk (a test score for risk factors that can change over time) were added as covariates (extra factors held constant statistically to see what was left over), most of the planning items stopped predicting recidivism. Only the accommodation score remained significant. The motivation item is the clearest version of this problem. A therapist who already saw a man as more settled and more engaged would reasonably write him a fuller plan and rate him as more motivated. In that case the plan and the outcome share a common cause in the man’s presentation.
Applying it to this workbook

Everything the two studies scored was written by a paid coordinator days before release, about a man who had already been observed by staff for months, for a report that a parole board would go on to read. Every plan in this library is instead written by the reader himself, alone, on his own initiative, at any point after the programme has ended, for nobody’s review. The finding says planning quality once tracked lower reoffending in that professionally supported setting. Whether a self-directed workbook completed without a coordinator, a parole board or months of observed behaviour reproduces the pattern was never tested.
Using this in a session

A facilitator can tell a client that better planning tracked better outcomes in the published research. The statement is accurate, and he was already told it in the preamble and both reference documents. A facilitator should not present the workbook in front of him as validated by that evidence, because the instrument that scored those plans was never applied to a document like his. The workbook’s value rests on the reasoning already given in the preamble’s “why bother writing any of this down”.

If you are the person doing the workbook, the same caution applies to it. The research found that planning quality once tracked a better outcome in a professionally prepared, professionally supervised plan. It has not shown that completing this workbook yourself goes with the same outcome. That does not reduce the workbook’s value, which depends on the preamble’s reasoning whether or not anybody else ever reads what you write in it.
